newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook-Volatile coffee seen at centre stage.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook-Volatile coffee seen at centre stage.

text.p: Coffee should attract most trading interest on London's soft commodity markets this week as nervous dealers prepare for the approach of Brazil's frost season, market sources said on Monday.
Supply concerns in key producing countries were likely to form the background for movements in cocoa and white sugar, they said.
In coffee, the robustas market was suffering from a lack of strong upward momentum although analysts said the charts pointed to a mildly bullish picture.
While supply prospects remained weak, London could draw strength from New York's arabicas market ahead of Brazil's frost season. June and July were viewed as the most critical months.
Arabicas jumped by as much as 16 percent last week, fuelled by concerns over Latin American supply and low consumer stocks.
Fresh supplies from Colombia and Central America are tight due to seasonal factors and heavy sales already made by producers to take advantage of the rally in prices.
Analysts said the gains could be sustained before this year's frosts.
"What goes up has to come down but in this case nobody is willing to sell because the market could rally again," said one trader.
Any attempt by the London market to rally has been consistently stalled by scale-up hedge selling by origins but the downside still looks comfortably supported by trade and roaster buying.
The immediate target faced by the benchmark July robusta contract is resistance at $1,705, after which it will have to fill a chart gap between $1,705 and $1,730.

In white sugar, the fortunes of New York should set the pace for London as market players adjust their July positions in light of the surprisingly large delivery of south Brazilian raws and the absence of Thai cargoes.

"Whites seem to be one step back from the raws activity at the moment...but there's nothing to say what the whites are going to do," said a trader, adding that one large receiver might try to pressure July raws lower.
If New York moved lower interest could also pick up in the August/July arbitrage, which has seen a lack of activity in recent sessions, he said.
Traders said London's nearby August contract should see a continuation of last week's light trade buying, which would keep prices broadly steady and above support.
Dry weather conditions in Europe could reduce the supply of quality white sugar from the 1996/97 season.
In cocoa, traders said London's key July contract should continue its battle with 980 stg support after last week's dive to 981, nearly a one-month low.
If the position headed below that level the weakness could trigger a wave of more losses as the next support was unlikely to emerge until 960, they said.
July dipped below the psychological 1,000 mark for the first time since April 10 as speculators unloaded cocoa on perceptions of mounting supplies.
A spate of crop data released last week points to a much weaker market. Ivorian supplies are expected to be much higher than first thought.
Brokers GNI and the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) both revised down their 1996/97 production deficit forecasts last week.

Independent technical analyst Elli Gifford said on Friday while July could break below 980 stg, the fall could be short-lived and the market could still rise again as it looked oversold in the short term.
"There's no clear sign the market is going to break down. It's due for a rally up again," she said.
-- Jeremy Smith, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
